A.title: Loser-pays-by-default tribunal rule, with a small-landlord safe harbour
A.answer: Keep the tribunal and the 1 April 2027 start, but change the cost rule. The housing ministry, through the tribunal rules, would make landlords bear their own legal costs of a service charge challenge unless the tribunal finds the leaseholder's case unreasonable [s1]. Leaseholders recover their own costs when they win [s1]. Small landlords get standard forms and a free template, so the paperwork does not bury them. Councils and housing associations keep the later 2028 date [s1]. We would know it worked if tribunal data show challenges rising, fewer leaseholders dropping cases over cost, and no rise in small-landlord complaints. Propertymark's survey found 89% of leaseholders say unfair charges are hard to challenge [s2].

B.title: Let each building's leaseholders approve the budget before billing
B.answer: The landlord stops being sole judge of its own bills. In each building, a leaseholder board, elected by the flat owners, approves the annual service charge budget before any demand goes out, and the landlord's agent reports to it. Landlords still cannot pass on dispute legal costs without tribunal approval from 1 April 2027 [s1], but disputes become rarer because bills are agreed first. Who: the government writes this into the coming Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill [s1]. How we'd know: fewer tribunal challenges, and the share of leaseholders calling unfair charges hard to challenge, 89% in a trade body survey [s2], falls. 31 simulated citizens backed checking charges before billing.
